summary: Describes a set of private SIP headers used by the 3rd Generation Partnership Project, along with where they apply, which is limited to particular environments. They carry things such as charging data and information about the networks a call crosses. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7315.

eli5.summary: Mobile phone networks stick extra private notes on call-setup messages, such as who pays and which networks it crossed. This note lists those notes. It was later replaced by RFC 7315.

questions: how does charging work in sip networks
subtitle: Private headers for 3GPP mobile SIP networks carrying charging, roaming, and network information.

tldr.problem: 3GPP mobile networks need to track call charging, identify which network a roaming subscriber is using, and pass access network details (like cell ID) through SIP call setup, but standard SIP headers cannot carry this private information.
tldr.mechanism: Defines six private headers (P-headers) for SIP: P-Associated-URI (identity lists), P-Called-Party-ID (which URI a call reached), P-Visited-Network-ID (which visited network is serving a roamer), P-Access-Network-Info (access technology and cell ID), P-Charging-Function-Addresses (where to send billing records), and P-Charging-Vector (charging correlation IDs).
tldr.outcome: 3GPP networks adopted these extensions in their IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem) architecture, later standardized more broadly in RFC 7315.

today: RFC 7315 superseded this RFC with an updated and consolidated version. Both documents define the same private headers for 3GPP networks, though RFC 7315 reflects more recent 3GPP specifications.

sections.title: Private Headers for 3GPP Networks
sections.content:
The 3GPP consortium designed SIP extensions to support their IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), which delivers voice, video, and messaging over IP in mobile networks. Standard SIP headers could not carry the information 3GPP networks needed. This RFC documents six private (P-header) extensions that are applicable only within 3GPP networks and similar closed environments where all nodes are trusted.

These headers are not suitable for the general Internet. They assume a network where all proxies are operated by the same provider or by trusted partners, business relationships are established, and internal integrity protection exists.
sections.eli5: When a call happens in a mobile network, the network wants to put extra information in the SIP message (like who should be charged and which network the phone is using) that the normal phone call headers do not support.

sections.title: The Six P-Headers
sections.content:
P-Associated-URI returns a list of other SIP addresses that the registrar has associated with a user, sent in the 200 OK response to a REGISTER request. This lets the user know what identities the network has allocated to them.

P-Called-Party-ID carries the original request URI before a proxy retargeted the call to the contact address. This tells the receiving phone which of its multiple registered addresses was actually dialed.

P-Visited-Network-ID identifies the visited network that is serving a roaming subscriber, sent from the visited network toward the home network. It uses a text string that both networks understand (often based on the visited network's domain name).

P-Access-Network-Info describes the access technology a user agent is using (for example, 3GPP UTRAN or IEEE 802.11) and may include cell identity or location information. The user agent inserts this; it is typically deleted by the home network proxy before forwarding outside the network.

P-Charging-Function-Addresses contains IP addresses of charging entities (for offline and online charging) that receive billing records from all proxies in the transaction. There may be multiple addresses for redundancy.

P-Charging-Vector correlates charging records across multiple proxies by carrying a globally unique charging identifier (ICID) and interoperator identifiers (IOI) that track which networks are involved in a call.
sections.eli5: Each header carries a different type of private information: one lists the user's phone numbers, one says which network is serving you, one holds cell location, one lists where to send the bill, and one has a unique call ID for billing.

sections.title: How P-Headers Are Used
sections.content:
P-Associated-URI is inserted by a registrar in a REGISTER response, and the user agent reads it. P-Called-Party-ID is inserted by a proxy in the home network that is retargeting a request and carries the original request URI to the receiving phone. P-Visited-Network-ID is inserted by proxies in visited networks to identify themselves to the home network, and may be encrypted so only the home network can read it. P-Access-Network-Info is inserted by a user agent and is stripped by the home network proxy to prevent disclosure outside the network.

P-Charging-Function-Addresses and P-Charging-Vector are inserted by proxies when first received (or modified as the message traverses the network). Proxies must delete these headers when forwarding messages outside the home network administrative domain to maintain privacy and prevent unauthorized charging systems from being contacted.
sections.eli5: Each header appears at a different stage of the call: the user gets a list of their addresses after registering, proxies add the called number and billing info as the call goes through, and sensitive headers are deleted before the message leaves the home network.

sections.title: Trust and Privacy
sections.content:
These headers expose sensitive information: phone numbers, location (cell ID), and billing relationships. The RFC emphasizes that they are intended only for closed networks where transitive trust exists between the home network and visited networks, and where integrity protection (using IPsec or TLS) is in place.

User agents sending P-Access-Network-Info must trust the network to delete the header before it leaves the domain. Networks receiving these headers must delete them when forwarding outside the trust domain. Without such protections, eavesdroppers could collect a user's registered identities, location, or access network details.
sections.eli5: This information should only travel inside a single company's network or between partners who trust each other. It must not be sent over the public internet.
